blocks.html:
What are we protecting, from whom, and how would we even know if we'd succeeded?

Begin with a system you can describe, then ask what a failure would harm. This chapter gives names to the protection goals and introduces the learning map used throughout the book. The first paper task starts your dossier.
What this chapter covers

By the end you should be able to:

  • Define information security and explain the CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity, availability.
  • Explain when those three can conflict, and what "balancing CIA" means in practice.
  • Say what a security control is, and what defence in depth buys you.
  • Walk through the phases of an attack, and explain why a defender studies them.
  • Distinguish ethical security work from malicious hacking, and see where the line sits.
Security is a property, not a product

You cannot buy security in a box. There is no single product, no switch, no certificate that makes a system "secure." Security is not a thing a system has. It is a property of how the whole system behaves, including the people using it. A bank vault with the door propped open is not secure no matter how thick the steel. A perfectly configured server whose administrator uses "password1" is not secure either. Security depends on how those choices interact. A weakness may expose one asset while other controls limit the damage.

That is why this book keeps returning to a defender's habit of mind rather than a checklist. Checklists go stale. The habit of asking "what am I protecting, from whom, and how would I know if it failed?" does not.
The CIA triad

Almost everything in information security can be traced back to protecting one of three properties of information. Together they are called the CIA triad (no relation to the agency).

Confidentiality is keeping information from those who should not see it. When you think of "security," this is usually what comes to mind: secrets stay secret. Encryption, access controls, and passwords are all, at heart, confidentiality mechanisms. A confidentiality failure is a leak: data ending up in the wrong hands.

Integrity is keeping information correct and un-tampered. It is less obvious than confidentiality but often matters more. If an attacker cannot read your bank balance but can change it, you have a worse problem than a leak. Integrity mechanisms let you detect or prevent unauthorised change. A hospital needs to trust that a patient's recorded blood type is the one a doctor entered, not one an attacker altered.

Availability is keeping information and systems there when they are needed. A system nobody can reach is no more useful than one that was deleted. Availability is the property attacked by a denial-of-service, threatened by a single point of failure, and protected by backups, redundancy, and capacity planning. It is the property people forget until the day the system is down and the business stops.

Balancing CIA

The CIA properties can conflict, but they do not inevitably work against each other. A tested backup can improve both integrity and availability. Well-managed access can protect confidentiality while helping authorised users find the right information.

Trade-offs arise in particular designs. Extra approval steps may delay urgent access. More replicas improve availability but create more copies to protect. Preventing every change would preserve an old record while making a booking system unusable. Ask which harm matters, who is affected, and what evidence shows the control meets the need. A hospital's emergency-access arrangement can be different from a newspaper's embargo process without either abandoning security.

A fourth idea often sits alongside the triad: non-repudiation, the property that someone cannot credibly deny having done something. An audit trail and a digital signature can support a claim about an action. They still depend on trustworthy identity binding, key control and records. An account identifier alone does not prove which human acted or settle a dispute.
Controls and defence in depth

A security control is anything you put between an asset and a threat to reduce risk: a password, a firewall, a locked door, a policy, a training session, a backup. Controls come in familiar flavours: some prevent (a lock stops entry), some detect (an alarm notices it), and some correct (a backup restores what was lost). A good defence uses all three, because prevention eventually fails.

This is the idea the book is named for. Defence in depth means never trusting a single control to be enough. You assume each layer will fail, and you put another behind it. A castle did not rely on the outer wall alone. It had a moat, then a wall, then a gate, then an inner keep, so that breaching one defence still left the attacker facing the next. A modern system is the same: a firewall and patched software and least-privilege accounts and monitoring and backups. Layers reduce dependence on any one control. Shared credentials, a common administrator or a shared power supply can still defeat several layers together.

This is the practical face of assume breach. If you assume the attacker will get past your first control, you stop asking "is this wall strong enough?" and start asking "when this fails, what catches it?" That question builds better systems than the search for one perfect wall ever could.
The phases of an attack

To defend against attackers, you have to understand how they work. You are not learning this to imitate them. You study each step to see what it needs, so you can take that away. Most intrusions move through recognisable phases:

  1. Reconnaissance. The attacker gathers information about the target from the outside: who works there, what systems they run, what's exposed. Quiet, often legal, and easy to overlook.
  2. Scanning. They probe the target directly for live systems, open ports, and running services, mapping the attack surface. In this book you can reason from supplied observations without probing any real system.
  3. Gaining access. They exploit a weakness (a flaw, a weak password, a tricked user) to get a foothold.
  4. Maintaining access. They entrench, so a reboot or a changed password doesn't lock them out.
  5. Clearing tracks. They cover their trail, deleting logs and hiding activity to delay discovery.

Read that list as a defender and each phase becomes an opportunity. Reconnaissance can be made harder by exposing less. Scanning can be detected. Access can be denied with patching and strong authentication. Persistence and track-clearing can be spotted by monitoring that the attacker cannot fully erase. Understanding the attacker's process is where a defender's leverage comes from.
Ethical hacking, and the line

Much of what you'll learn in this book is, in mechanism, identical to what an attacker does: scanning systems, cracking passwords, capturing traffic. The difference is permission and purpose. An ethical practitioner acts with the owner's authorisation, within an agreed scope, to find and fix weaknesses before a real attacker exploits them. Unapproved testing may be unlawful and can harm others. Treat explicit permission and agreed scope as prerequisites, not optional courtesy.

This is where the old "hats" come from. A white hat works with authorisation, to find and fix. A black hat breaks in for their own gain or to cause harm. A grey hat acts without permission while believing the intent is good. Good intentions do not move the line. What separates the three is authorisation.

That line is sharp and it matters. Practise only in an environment you own or are explicitly authorised to use. The skills are dual-use. Your professionalism is what makes them defensive.
Try it yourself

Begin with the fictional, paper-based Harbour case. Optional technical practice requires an explicitly authorised environment with checked boundaries. The practice appendix explains why a VM, NAT connection or container does not itself establish isolation.
A lifecycle to revisit

Use seven activities as a learning map: design, harden, detect, respond, recover, investigate, and audit/learn. People and decisions run through all seven. Activities overlap: evidence collection can begin during response, and a recovery test can reveal a design flaw before any breach occurs. This is the book's teaching map, not a mandated sequence. NIST's incident-response guidance places incident work within continuing risk management.
Where this connects

The CIA triad and defence in depth are the lenses for the whole book. Almost every later control exists to protect one leg of the triad or to add one more layer. The next chapter begins the technical detail, looking at where software goes wrong and the malware that walks through the gaps.
Questions to consider

1. Give a real situation where confidentiality matters most, one where integrity matters most, and one where availability matters most. Use three different examples.
  2. "More security is always better." Describe one case where tightening security actually made things worse. What was traded away?
  3. Why would a defender bother learning the phases of an attack? What specifically do you gain by understanding how an attacker thinks?
Map an asset

Read Harbour's facts. In 10 minutes, choose one asset and write a four-column row: harm, plausible threat, control, and evidence that the control works. Then name one residual failure. A good row connects a specific harm to a test; “use encryption” without saying what it protects is not enough.

Case inputs and checks: Harbour dossier.

A software flaw can give an attacker a foothold. What happens next depends on the access and controls around it.

Software vulnerabilities, stolen credentials and deceptive messages can each give an attacker a foothold. This chapter concentrates on software flaws and malware, then uses a historical breach to show how several failures can connect. Chapter 10 returns to the criminal market and the evidence left behind.
What this chapter covers

By the end you should be able to:

  • Distinguish design flaws from implementation flaws, and explain attack surface.
  • Explain what CVE and CWE are, and how vulnerability disclosure works (responsible disclosure, zero-day).
  • Classify the main families of malware: viruses, worms, spyware, adware, trojans, RATs, ransomware, rootkits, and botnets.
  • Explain how a trojan and a botnet actually work, and how we detect and prevent them.
  • Trace how a real breach chains several of these together.
Where flaws come from

Software fails in two ways, and the distinction matters because they are fixed differently.

A design flaw is a mistake in the plan. The software does what it was designed to do, and the design itself is insecure. A system that emails you your own password in plain text has no bug. It works as intended, and the intention is the problem. Design flaws are expensive because fixing them means changing the plan, often after everything has been built on top of it.

An implementation flaw is a mistake in the building. The design was sound, but somewhere in the code a programmer made an error: mishandled a length, trusted an input they shouldn't have, forgot a check. Implementation flaws are one reason software needs patching. A patch may also change an insecure design; the categories help us reason but can overlap.

Every flaw is only a threat if an attacker can reach it. This brings us to attack surface: the sum of all the points where an attacker could try to get in. Every open port, every input field, every feature, every piece of installed software adds to it. A defender's instinct, seen already in the last chapter, is to reduce attack surface: turn off what you don't use, close what you don't need, and you shrink the number of doors an attacker can try. Attack surface is not fixed. It grows every time you add a feature, install software, or connect a new system, which is why security is never "done."
Naming the weaknesses: CVE and CWE

When there are millions of flaws across the world's software, you need a way to talk about them precisely. Two catalogues do this. A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) is a unique identifier for a vulnerability record, which can identify affected products and versions. A shared flaw may affect more than one product; the identifier gives people a common reference. A CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) is one level up: a category of type of flaw ("improper input validation," "use after free") that recurs across many products. CVEs are the individual cases; CWEs are the patterns behind them. The CVE programme and CWE catalogue describe their different purposes.

Disclosure and the zero-day

When a researcher finds a flaw, coordinated vulnerability disclosure aims to get useful information to affected parties while reducing harm. A researcher reports through an authorised channel and coordinates with the vendor or a relevant response team. Publication timing must account for active exploitation, user protection and unresponsive vendors; it is not always “wait until patched”. CERT/CC's disclosure guide explains the roles and trade-offs.

A zero-day vulnerability is commonly discussed as a flaw for which defenders do not yet have an available fix, often before public disclosure. Distinguish the vulnerability from a zero-day exploit or attack that uses it. Terminology varies, so describe whether the vendor knew, whether a patch existed and whether exploitation was observed. Layered controls matter when patching cannot yet remove the exposure.
Malware: a field guide

Malware (malicious software) is the general term for any program written to do harm. The families are worth knowing because they spread and survive differently, and each difference is a place to defend.

Viruses and worms

A virus attaches itself to a legitimate file or program and spreads when that host is run and shared. It needs a carrier and, usually, a human to move it. A macro virus hides in the scripting built into documents (a spreadsheet or word-processor file), which is why "enable macros?" is a question worth treating with suspicion.

A worm is the more dangerous cousin: it spreads on its own, across the network, without needing a host file or a human to carry it. The 1988 Morris Worm, one of the first, showed the pattern that still holds: self-propagating code can move faster than any human response. For a defender, a worm's fuel is connectivity and unpatched systems, so segmentation and patching are what starve it.

Spyware, adware, and the willing click

Not all malware exploits a software flaw. Spyware collects information (keystrokes, browsing, credentials) and reports it back. Adware forces unwanted advertising and often tracks you to do it. A great deal of malware needs no vulnerability at all: it needs the user to agree, to click "install," to run the attachment, to grant the permission. This is the theme that returns in the human-factors chapter: the most patched system in the world can still be undone by one willing click.
Trojans, RATs, and botnets

A trojan horse is malware disguised as something desirable: a game, a cracked application, a useful tool. The user runs it willingly, and while it may even do what it claims, it also does something else. A Remote Access Trojan (RAT) is a nasty variant: it hands the attacker remote control of the machine (files, webcam, keystrokes, the lot) as though they were sitting at it.

Scale this up and you get a botnet: a network of many compromised machines ("bots") under one attacker's control, taking orders from a command-and-control server. A botnet's owner can rent it out to send spam, mine cryptocurrency, or overwhelm a target with a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack. The infamous Zeus family, for example, turned huge numbers of ordinary PCs into a credential-stealing network. The defender's insight is that a botnet's value is aggregate. No single infected machine matters much, which is why individual users underestimate the cost of being compromised.

Ransomware can encrypt data and disrupt services; attackers may also steal data and threaten to publish it. Tested, protected backups support recovery but cannot undo disclosure. Paying does not guarantee either restoration or deletion of stolen copies. Response therefore includes containment, assessment of exposed data and recovery, not just obtaining a decryption key. CISA's ransomware guide covers these connected risks.
Rootkits: hiding in the floor

A rootkit is malware that subverts a low level of the system (the operating system, or below it) so that it can hide everything above. By compromising the layer the rest of the system trusts to report the truth, a rootkit can make its own files, processes, and network connections invisible to the tools you'd normally use to find them. This is why compromised machines are often rebuilt from scratch rather than "cleaned": once you can't trust the floor you're standing on, you can't trust anything it tells you.
Defending against malware

No single control stops all of this. That is why the book argues for layered defence. Signature-based detection recognises known patterns; other endpoint techniques look at behaviour or suspicious activity. Neither guarantees detection of an unfamiliar attack, so endpoint protection must be one layer among many. Patching closes the flaws worms and exploits need. Least privilege stops a compromised program reaching everything. Controls limit what software is allowed to run. User education targets the willing click. Monitoring catches the intrusion that gets through anyway. "We have antivirus" is not a security strategy. It is one thin layer, and a defender who relies on it alone has assumed the breach won't happen.
How it comes together: a real breach

Real attacks rarely use one flaw. They chain several. The 2013 Target breach is a classic worked example. Attackers first stole network credentials from a third-party contractor (a heating-and-cooling vendor with access to Target's systems). They used that foothold to reach the retail network and installed point-of-sale malware (the "BlackPOS" family) that scraped card data from checkout terminals. They exfiltrated tens of millions of card records while warning signs went unheeded. Read it as a defender and every stage is a control that could have caught it: tighter vendor access, network segmentation, restricted software execution, and someone acting on the alerts. Several controls offered possible opportunities to interrupt that chain. Which would have worked depends on implementation and timing. The 2014 Senate staff analysis discusses possible missed opportunities using the public reporting then available; it is not proof of a unique counterfactual.
Play it

Incident Zero, a free, print-and-play security game, has a Hardening module where you spend a limited budget on layered defences and then a pentester attacks. It's the fastest way to feel why one control is never enough, and why "we have antivirus" is not a security strategy. → incidentzero.retroverse.studio
Where this connects

The introduction laid out the phases of an attack, and this chapter fills in the "gaining access" phase. Stolen credentials, as in the Target breach, are the entry point the authentication chapter is about. Botnets and the criminal economy behind malware return in cybercrime, botnets and forensics.
Questions to consider

1. What's the difference between a design flaw and an implementation flaw? Give an everyday (non-software) analogy for each.
  2. A worm and a trojan both spread, but they rely on different things. What does each one need to succeed, and which is easier to defend against?
  3. Skim the Target breach. Write your one-sentence guess at the single change that would most likely have stopped it.
Trace a possible path

In 10 minutes, connect Harbour's shared administrator credential, export permissions and backup credentials into a possible attack path. Label the path hypothetical. Name two places to interrupt it and one observation needed before claiming this was what happened. Do not invent a malware infection when the supplied evidence only records account activity.

Case inputs and checks: Harbour dossier.

A successful login establishes an identity claim. The next question is what that account is allowed to do.

At Harbour, Rae needs to amend a booking but should not be able to export every participant's details. Checking who signs in and limiting what they can do are separate controls. This chapter follows both, including how systems protect password verifiers, recover accounts and end compromised sessions.
What this chapter covers

By the end you should be able to:

  • Distinguish identification, authentication, and authorisation, and explain mutual authentication and ID proofing.
  • Explain the three factors of authentication and what multi-factor authentication actually adds.
  • Describe how a system stores credentials: cryptographic hashing, and why we add salt.
  • Explain Windows / NTLM authentication at a high level and why it matters in practice.
  • Analyse password attacks (dictionary, brute-force, rainbow tables) and the defences that beat each one: salting, lockout, length.
Three words people mix up

These three terms are used loosely in everyday speech and precisely in security, and the precision matters.

Identification is a claim: you state who you are (a username, an account number, a name). It is just an assertion, and on its own it proves nothing.

Authentication is the proof of that claim: you demonstrate that you are who you said. Typing the password that matches the username is authentication. This is the step attackers most want to defeat, because a successful fake here makes everything downstream trust them.

Authorisation is what happens after: given that we now believe who you are, what are you allowed to do? A verified user is not an all-powerful one. Authentication gets you through the door. Authorisation decides which rooms you may enter. Keeping these separate lets a system trust who you are while still limiting what you can do. This is the principle of least privilege in action.

Two refinements are worth naming. Mutual authentication is when both sides prove their identity. Not only does the server check you, but you (or your software) check the server, so you're not handing your credentials to an impostor. ID proofing is the harder, real-world problem of establishing identity in the first place. How does a bank know the person opening an account is who they claim, before any password exists? Authentication verifies a claim you set up earlier. Proofing is how that claim was trusted to begin with.
The three factors

How can you prove who you are? Every method falls into one of three factors:

  • Something you know: a password, a PIN, the answer to a question.
  • Something you have: a phone, a hardware token, a smart card.
  • Something you are: a fingerprint, a face, a voice (biometrics).

Passwords are widely used because they need little special hardware, but guessing, reuse and phishing make them risky on their own. Long, unique passwords generated and stored with a password manager reduce guessing and reuse. Arbitrary complexity rules can encourage predictable substitutions; rate limiting addresses repeated online guesses. Neither stops a user submitting a password to an impostor.

Multi-factor authentication

One important improvement is to require more than one factor: multi-factor authentication (MFA). The power comes from combining categories: a password (know) plus a code from your phone (have) means stealing the password alone is no longer enough. The "have" factor takes many forms: a one-time code, a hardware token or key fob, or a smart card carrying a chip that proves possession. The "are" factor, biometrics, is convenient and hard to forget, but carries a permanent trade-off: you can change a breached password, but you cannot change your fingerprint. MFA is strong, but it is not magic. An attacker may still phish a one-time code or trick a user into approving a prompt. The type of MFA matters. Passkeys and suitable security keys bind an authentication response to the legitimate service, resisting a fake login site in a way a relayed one-time code does not. Their enrolment, device protection and recovery paths still need care. A biometric often unlocks an authenticator locally rather than being sent to the website as a password. NIST's authenticator guidance distinguishes these mechanisms.
What a system actually stores

Here is the idea that surprises most people, and it is the hinge of the whole chapter: a well-built system does not store your password. If it did, anyone who stole the database (or any administrator) would know every user's secret.

Instead, the system stores a password verifier produced by a purpose-built password-hashing scheme. At login it derives a verifier from the supplied password and stored parameters, then compares the result. A cryptographic hash is designed to resist inversion, but attackers can still guess inputs.

The scheme must make each guess expensive through a suitable work factor, and often memory cost. A fast general-purpose hash alone is not appropriate password storage. Libraries implementing schemes such as Argon2id handle these details; do not invent a scheme from hash primitives. OWASP's password-storage guidance explains the choice and parameters.

Windows and NTLM

Windows' legacy NTLM authentication is useful optional background. It uses password-derived credential material in a challenge/response scheme. Stolen NTLM hash material may enable pass-the-hash authentication without recovering the plaintext password. Treat it as a credential, not as harmless scrambled data. It is not a model for designing a new password store. Microsoft's NTLM overview describes the protocol, and NIST's threat guidance includes reuse of stolen authentication material.
Attacking passwords

If attackers can get the hashes but can't reverse them, how do they recover passwords? They don't reverse the hash. They guess, hash each guess, and look for a match.

A dictionary attack works through a list of likely passwords (common words, previously leaked passwords, predictable patterns) because real people rarely choose randomly. A brute-force attack tries every possible combination. For a finite candidate space it can exhaust every candidate, but the work may be infeasible. Length helps when it adds unpredictability; a long, well-known phrase can still be guessed early. The accelerator is a rainbow table: a giant precomputed lookup of hashes for enormous numbers of candidate passwords, so the attacker trades storage for speed and skips the recomputation.

The fix: salt

Rainbow tables have one fatal weakness, and the fix is elegant. Before hashing, the system adds a unique random value, a salt, to each password, and stores the salt alongside the hash. Now two users with the same password have different hashes, and the attacker's precomputed rainbow table, built without your specific salt, is worthless. Salting doesn't make any single password harder to guess. It prevents useful reuse of the same precomputed table across different salts. The attacker must work separately for each salt. The password-hashing scheme's cost settings, not the salt alone, make each guess expensive.

Distinguish online guessing against a login service from offline guessing against stolen verifiers. Login rate limits and lockouts do not slow an attacker working on their own copy. Long unique passwords, proper verifier storage and protection of the database address that different threat.
The maths is rarely the weakest link

Everything above assumes the attacker has to defeat authentication. Often they go around it. A keylogger records the password as you type it, before any hashing happens. Social engineering just asks. A convincing email or phone call, and the user hands the secret over. Sniffing captures credentials sent in the clear across a network (which returns in the network-security chapter). And stealing the password file itself gives the attacker the hashes to work on at leisure. The recurring lesson of this book applies here: the cryptography is rarely what fails. The people and the plumbing around it are.
A word on single sign-on

One more idea you'll meet: single sign-on (SSO) lets you authenticate once and gain access to many systems, and reduced sign-on is a lighter version of the same convenience. Users love it, and it improves security in one way: fewer passwords means less reuse and fewer sticky notes. But it concentrates risk: a compromised identity provider or session may expose several services. SSO must still enforce per-service permissions, restricted administration and revocation; it need not give every account access to everything. Protect the identity provider and recovery process with appropriate MFA.
Permissions and recovery are part of the design

A receptionist may need to amend one booking without being allowed to export every participant's details. Enforce that rule on the server for each action, not just by hiding a button. Review access when duties change or people leave.

Recovery is another entry path. A help desk that bypasses all checks when a caller sounds urgent can undermine strong login controls. Plan an independent identity check, recovery credentials where appropriate, and revocation of affected sessions. Changing a password alone does not prove that every existing session has ended.
Where this connects

The hashing this chapter relies on is the subject of the next chapter, cryptography. Sniffing for credentials reappears in network security, when we capture packets on the wire. And stolen credentials, as in the Target breach, are how many intrusions begin, a thread running back to software security and malware.
Questions to consider

1. If a website is breached, why is it so much better for you that they stored a salted hash of your password rather than the password itself?
  2. MFA asks for a second factor. Give a realistic example where MFA still fails, where the attacker gets in anyway. What does that tell you about relying on it?
  3. Why does adding salt defeat a rainbow table, when it doesn't make any single password harder to guess?
Separate login from permission

In 10 minutes, write the actions Mara, Rae and a volunteer should be allowed to perform at Harbour. Include one denied action for each role. Add a test for account recovery and session revocation. Success means a legitimate login does not silently confer bulk-export or administrator rights.

A sound cipher should remain secure when its design is public and only the key is secret.

Cryptography can protect information sent through an untrusted network, but different operations solve different problems. Encrypting a booking, hashing an export and signing a message do not provide interchangeable assurances. You do not need to derive the algorithms here; you need to identify the protection, its assumptions and the systems it depends on.
What this chapter covers

By the end you should be able to:

  • Explain the difference between an algorithm and a key, and state Kerckhoff's principle.
  • Distinguish symmetric (one-key) from asymmetric (two-key) cryptography and say what each is good for.
  • Explain hashing vs encryption, and where digital signatures fit.
  • Reason about attacks: brute-forcing small key spaces, known-plaintext and chosen-plaintext attacks.
The algorithm and the key

Every cipher has two parts, and telling them apart is the foundation of everything else. The algorithm is the method: the fixed procedure for scrambling and unscrambling. The key is the secret input that steers it: the particular setting that turns readable plaintext into scrambled ciphertext and back. The same algorithm with a different key produces different output. The set of all possible keys is the key space, and its size is one measure of a cipher's strength: the more keys an attacker would have to try, the better.

Here is where beginners' intuition usually goes wrong. It feels safer to keep the algorithm secret too. Surely hiding the method helps? Kerckhoff's principle says the opposite, and it is one of the most important ideas in the whole field:

A cryptosystem should be secure even if everything about it, except the key, is public knowledge.

In other words, the security must rest entirely on the secrecy of the key, never on the secrecy of the algorithm. This sounds counter-intuitive until you see why it's a strength. Keeping a design secret can limit independent review without demonstrating that the design is sound. If secrecy of the algorithm is the only protection, disclosure removes it. A public algorithm, published and attacked by the world's cryptographers for years, has earned its trust the hard way. This is why every cipher you should trust (the ones protecting your web traffic, your messages, your disk) has an openly published algorithm and keeps only the key secret. "Secret sauce" cryptography is a warning sign.
Symmetric cryptography: one shared key

The oldest and simplest arrangement is symmetric (or one-key) cryptography: the same key both encrypts and decrypts. If you and I share a secret key, I encrypt with it, you decrypt with it, and anyone without it sees only noise. Symmetric ciphers are fast and efficient, which is why they do the heavy lifting of bulk encryption: encrypting a whole disk, a database, or a stream of network traffic.

Symmetric cryptography has one stubborn problem, and it's not the maths: key distribution. Before we can communicate securely, we both need the same secret key. But how do I get it to you securely in the first place? If we could already send secrets safely, we wouldn't need the encryption. For two people who have never met, sharing a key over an untrusted network is the problem the whole system was meant to solve. For centuries this was cryptography's central limitation.
Asymmetric cryptography: a key you can publish

Asymmetric cryptography uses a mathematically related public/private key pair. The public key can be shared; the private key must be protected. Different schemes perform different jobs. Do not assume every pair can encrypt, decrypt and sign interchangeably.

With a public-key encryption scheme, a sender encrypts to the recipient's public key and the recipient decrypts using the private key. But the sender must establish that this really is the recipient's key. Publishing a key does not by itself solve the problem of authenticating it.

A digital signature is a separate operation: a signing algorithm uses a private key, and a verification algorithm uses the corresponding public key. Signing is not generally “encrypting with the private key”. Verification checks the signature against the message. A valid signature supports a claim about the signing key, subject to trustworthy key identity and control; it does not by itself prove a human's intent. NIST's Digital Signature Standard describes these distinct signing and verification operations.

Real systems often combine public-key techniques with fast symmetric protection. In a certificate-authenticated TLS connection, the browser checks the server's certificate and name, the parties establish traffic keys, and symmetric authenticated encryption protects the traffic. Modern key agreement can derive a shared secret rather than sending a symmetric key encrypted with the server's public key. TLS 1.3 separates these steps. If certificate validation fails, do not bypass the warning just to continue.
Hashing: one-way, and not encryption

A hash function is often grouped with cryptography but does something different, and the difference matters. Encryption is reversible. With the right key, decryption recovers the original. A cryptographic hash is deliberately one-way: it turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint that cannot be reversed to recover the input. You met this in the last chapter, where systems store the hash of a password rather than the password itself.

Encryption aims to protect confidentiality. A cryptographic hash gives a compact comparison value designed to make it infeasible to find a different input with the same digest. Collisions are mathematically possible; “every change must produce a different hash” is not the guarantee.

To check a downloaded file, compare its digest with an expected value obtained through a trusted channel. If an attacker replaces both the file and its advertised digest, comparison alone proves nothing about authenticity. A keyed message authentication code or a signature can add authentication under the relevant key assumptions.

Encryption alone also need not detect tampering. Authenticated encryption combines confidentiality with an integrity check, rejecting altered protected data. Use a maintained protocol or library rather than assembling your own combination. Key theft, a compromised endpoint or an authorised but malicious application session can still expose the plaintext.
Attacks, and the limits of weak crypto

Understanding how ciphers fail sharpens the intuition. The simplest failure is a key space too small to matter. The classic Caesar cipher shifts each letter by a fixed amount. But there are only twenty-five possible shifts, so an attacker tries them all in seconds. A monoalphabetic substitution cipher, where each letter maps to another, has an enormous key space yet still falls easily, because it leaks the structure of the language: letter frequencies survive the substitution, and 'e' is still the commonest letter. A big key space is necessary but not sufficient. A cipher can be broken by the patterns it fails to hide.

Cryptographers also reason about what an attacker gets to see. In a known-plaintext attack, the attacker has some plaintext and its matching ciphertext and uses the pair to attack the key. In the stronger chosen-plaintext attack, they can feed in plaintext of their choosing and study the output. A cipher worth trusting must withstand even an adversary with those advantages. That is why real ciphers are published and battered by experts rather than kept secret and hoped over.

Well-chosen modern cryptography can make direct cryptanalytic attacks impractical. Attackers may instead exploit the surrounding system. They steal the key from a poorly protected file, trick a user into revealing it, exploit a bug in the implementation of a sound algorithm, or take the data before it's encrypted or after it's decrypted. Even ransomware, which weaponises encryption against you, succeeds through the plumbing (how it gets in and what it can reach) rather than by breaking the cipher. The defender must examine both the cryptographic choice and its operating conditions; neither should be assumed correct merely because encryption is present.
Where this connects

Password verification uses the hashing ideas introduced in authentication. The encrypted tunnel a VPN builds rests on the symmetric, asymmetric, and key-exchange ideas here, as VPN and firewalls will show. And the secure connection behind every reputable website is the hybrid scheme described above, which returns in web security and data protection.
Questions to consider

1. Why is it a good thing that strong ciphers publish their algorithms openly?
  2. Symmetric crypto is faster; asymmetric solves key distribution. Sketch how a real system might use both.
  3. What's the practical difference between hashing a message and encrypting it? When would you want each?
Choose the protection

In 10 minutes, decide what protects Harbour's traffic, stored records and backup comparison values. Explain one limitation of each choice. Your answer should recognise that an application can export plaintext after login, and that a hash beside an editable file needs a separately trusted reference. Compare with the worked dossier only after making your choices.

blocks.html:
You can't protect everything equally, so you don't. Risk management is how a defender decides where the money and effort go.

Everything before this chapter was about how to defend: controls, cryptography, layered defence. This chapter is about where to spend the effort. It is the moment security stops being a technical subject and becomes a business one. No organisation has unlimited money, time, or patience, so a defender who tries to protect everything equally protects nothing well. Risk management is the discipline of deciding, honestly and defensibly, what to protect, how much to spend, and what to leave alone. It is also where "assume breach" turns into a budget.
What this chapter covers

By the end you should be able to:

  • Define risk, risk appetite, and explain why appetite varies between organisations.
  • Explain cost-benefit analysis and the difference between intrinsic and acquired value.
  • Calculate single loss expectancy (SLE) and annual loss expectancy (ALE), and use them to judge whether a control is worth it.
  • Describe the main risk treatments: avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept.
What risk actually is

In everyday speech "risk" means danger. In security it means something more precise and useful: risk is the combination of how likely something bad is and how much it would hurt if it happened. A useful shorthand is risk = likelihood × impact. Neither alone tells you much. A catastrophic event that almost never happens may be a smaller risk than a minor one that happens weekly. Treating them as equal, as a fear-driven approach does, wastes effort on the dramatic and ignores the routine.

Because risk is about likelihood and impact, it is always relative to a particular organisation. That is where risk appetite comes in: how much risk a given organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its goals. A hospital and a social-media start-up face different threats, value different things, and answer to different regulators, so they will rationally accept different risks. Risk appetite is a deliberate statement of how much uncertainty an organisation will live with. It is neither recklessness nor timidity. Two well-run companies facing the same threat can make opposite, equally defensible decisions. They should be able to explain the constraints behind those choices.
What are you protecting, and what's it worth?

You cannot judge a risk without knowing the value of what's at stake, and value is subtler than a price tag. An asset has intrinsic value (what it is worth in itself, like the replacement cost of a server) and acquired value (the worth it takes on from its role and context). A customer database might contain a few dollars of storage, but the acquired value (the trust, the regulatory exposure, the competitive harm if it leaked) can be enormous. Defenders who price only the intrinsic value under-protect the things that matter most, because the damage from losing information usually dwarfs the cost of the hardware holding it.

Once you can value what's at stake, you can do cost-benefit analysis: weigh what a control costs against the loss it prevents. This provides one input to a security decision. It has an uncomfortable implication people resist: sometimes the right answer is to not buy the control, because it costs more than the harm it prevents. That judgement is constrained by legal duties, safety and the organisation's stated limits. A positive financial return is not the only reason to protect people.
Putting numbers on it: SLE, ARO, ALE

To make cost-benefit concrete, security borrows a simple model from insurance. Three quantities do the work. Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) is how much one occurrence of the event would cost you. Annualised Rate of Occurrence (ARO) is how many times a year you expect it to happen, and it can be a fraction: 0.2 means once every five years. Annual Loss Expectancy (ALE) is the expected cost per year, SLE × ARO.

Here is a worked example. Suppose a breach of your customer database would cost about \$500,000 to clean up, notify, and recover from. That is the SLE. You judge such a breach might happen once every five years, so the ARO is 0.2. The annual loss expectancy is:

ALE = SLE × ARO = \$500,000 × 0.2 = \$100,000 per year.

That \$100,000 is what this risk "costs" you in expectation each year, and it's the number a control has to beat.
Is the control worth it?

Now you can judge a control honestly. Say better monitoring and encryption cost \$40,000 a year and would cut the breach rate to once every twenty years (ARO 0.05). The new annual loss expectancy becomes \$500,000 × 0.05 = \$25,000. So the control reduces your ALE from \$100,000 to \$25,000, a benefit of \$75,000 a year, for a cost of \$40,000. It saves you \$35,000 net, so it is worth buying.

For this financial model, a control has positive expected net benefit when the reduction in ALE exceeds its annual cost. That is not a complete acceptance rule for safety, privacy or regulatory obligations. Turn the numbers around and the answer flips. A \$50,000 control that only reduces an ALE from \$30,000 to \$5,000 loses you money, and buying it out of a vague sense that "more security is better" is the mistake this chapter exists to prevent.

Two honest cautions come with the arithmetic. First, notice that even after the good control, \$25,000 of annual risk remains: this is residual risk, the risk left over after treatment. You almost never reduce risk to zero, and pretending otherwise is how organisations get surprised. Second, these numbers are estimates: SLE and ARO are educated guesses, and some impacts (a ruined reputation, harm to people, loss of life) resist being priced at all. Treat quantitative risk analysis as a discipline for thinking clearly. The numbers structure the judgement; they do not replace it.
The four things you can do with a risk

Once a risk is identified and sized, you have four options. They are the vocabulary every security professional shares:

  • Avoid. Don't do the risky thing at all. Stop offering the feature, don't collect the data, close the exposure. This can remove the particular exposure, but may introduce other risks. It is often impractical because the activity is part of the business.
  • Mitigate. Reduce the likelihood or the impact with controls. This is most of what the rest of this book is about: patch, encrypt, segment, train, monitor. You rarely eliminate the risk; you shrink it to an acceptable size.
  • Transfer. Share specified financial consequences through insurance or a contract. Coverage, exclusions and provider obligations matter. Outsourcing does not automatically transfer your responsibility for customers or legal compliance.
  • Accept. Decide the risk is small enough, or the fix too costly, to live with it. This is a legitimate, deliberate choice, provided it's made consciously and by someone with the authority to make it. Record the owner, reasoning, residual exposure and review date. An unexamined risk is not the same as deliberate acceptance.

Organisations use resources with different purposes: the ASD Essential Eight sets out mitigation strategies and maturity expectations; ISO/IEC 27001 specifies an information-security management system; the NIST Cybersecurity Framework organises cybersecurity outcomes. They are not interchangeable pass/fail checklists. The NIST CSF provides a starting point for understanding outcomes and governance. Use the framework to structure evidence and responsibilities, then explain how the chosen treatment addresses the organisation's actual exposure.
Play it

Incident Zero's Audit & Compliance module has you score an organisation's controls pass/fail against a real framework, and then defend your judgement to the table. It turns the abstract choice between accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid into a call you have to argue for out loud. → incidentzero.retroverse.studio
Where this connects

The next chapter, incident and disaster planning, is what you do when a risk you accepted or mitigated happens anyway. Every control elsewhere in the book is a mitigation, and this chapter is how you decide which ones are worth deploying. A maturity assessment against a standard like the Essential Eight is this same risk-based reasoning, applied control by control.
Questions to consider

1. Two companies face the same threat but treat it differently. One buys insurance, one consciously accepts it. How can both be rational?
  2. A control costs \$50k/year and reduces an ALE of \$30k/year to \$5k/year. Should they buy it? Show your reasoning.
  3. Give a real risk your own organisation (or somewhere you've studied or worked) probably accepts rather than fixes. Why is that a defensible choice?
Calculate, then challenge

In 15 minutes, calculate Harbour's expected-loss reduction and net benefit for option A. Repeat for post-control annual rates 0.02 and 0.09. Then choose an affordable set of controls and record what it leaves unresolved. Success requires correct arithmetic, stated assumptions and a named risk owner; a positive estimate alone is not approval to ignore binding duties.

Case inputs and checks: Harbour dossier.
Take it to the AI

Optional: attempt the paper task first. Use only the fictional case, never real messages, credentials, personal information or internal logs. Check any external claims against the primary sources; do not deploy generated rules.

Act as a reviewer of my fictional Harbour risk decision. Identify the assumption most likely to change my conclusion. Use only the printed costs and estimates; do not invent product effectiveness. Ask one question, wait for my answer, then explain how I could obtain better evidence.

The question isn't whether something will go wrong, but whether you're ready when it does.

At Harbour, an unexpected login prompt and a bulk-export event arrive within minutes of each other. Who can suspend access, preserve the logs, talk to the service provider and decide what the centre tells participants? This chapter turns those questions into a response plan. Preparation and recovery tests belong before the first incident.
What this chapter covers

By the end you should be able to:

  • Distinguish incident response, business continuity, and disaster recovery.
  • Explain RTO and RPO and why they drive the plan.
  • Describe what a good incident response process looks like (detect → respond → recover → learn).
  • Explain the role of backups, alternate sites, and testing the plan.
When prevention runs out

Patching and access controls lower the chance of compromise. Detection, response and recovery reduce harm when prevention fails. They also help with mistakes and outages unrelated to an attacker.

Preparation means deciding authority, keeping contact information available, and testing recovery while there is time to correct a failure. A response plan should work when the usual administrator is absent and the primary communication system is unavailable.
Incident response: the lifecycle

An incident involves an actual or imminent threat to security. A suspicious event needs triage; staff should not wait for certainty before reporting it. A response process turns incomplete observations into proportionate action:

  • Detect and assess. Record the observation, time and affected service. Decide urgency and scope, distinguishing facts from assumptions.
  • Respond. Contain damage under assigned authority. Preserve useful evidence where feasible while restricting compromised access. Record actions that change or destroy evidence and why they were necessary.
  • Recover. Address the cause and persistence, restore or rebuild from an acceptable state, and validate access and integrity before reconnecting. A successful restore is not proof the attacker has been removed.
  • Learn. Review controls, decisions and communication. Assign improvements and check that they are completed.

These activities overlap. Evidence collection and analysis begin during response, not only after restoration. Do not indiscriminately wipe a system before consulting the response lead; equally, do not leave serious harm continuing solely to obtain perfect evidence. NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 places incident response within continuing risk management.

Two things make or break response in practice, and neither is technical. Roles must be decided in advance (who declares an incident, who talks to whom, who has the authority to take a critical system offline), because a crisis is the worst possible time to be working out the org chart. And communication must be planned: internal coordination, and the harder question of what you tell customers, regulators, and the public, and when.
Business continuity and disaster recovery

Two related disciplines sit alongside incident response, and people constantly confuse them.

Business continuity is the big picture: keeping the organisation running during a serious disruption of any kind, not just a cyberattack. If the office floods, the payroll system dies, or ransomware locks every file, how does the business keep serving customers and paying staff? It covers people, processes, premises, and priorities, the whole organisation's ability to function through a crisis.

Disaster recovery is the technical subset of that: restoring the IT systems and data after they've been lost or damaged. Business continuity asks "how does the company keep operating?"; disaster recovery asks "how do we get the systems and data back?" Recovery serves continuity (you restore the systems so the business can continue), but they are not the same plan, and an organisation needs both.
The two numbers that drive the plan: RTO and RPO

Disaster recovery turns on two deceptively simple targets, and getting them straight is the most useful thing in this chapter.

Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the target elapsed time for restoring an agreed service level after disruption. Set it within the organisation's maximum tolerable disruption, allowing for dependencies and validation. A trading platform's RTO might be minutes; an internal wiki's might be days.

Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is how much data you can afford to lose: the maximum tolerable gap between your last good backup and the moment of failure. An RPO of one hour means you can lose at most an hour's work; an RPO of a day means losing a day's is acceptable.

The RPO constrains your recovery design, including backup or replication frequency and the availability of usable recovery points. This is where plans contradict themselves. If a company declares an RPO of one hour but backs up only once a night, the plan is broken on its face: a failure just before the nightly backup could lose nearly twenty-four hours of data, not one. The stated goal and the actual practice don't match, and no one notices until the day it matters. Test the gap using a failure time near the end of the backup interval. A copied but corrupt or compromised backup does not meet the target. NIST's contingency-planning guidance helps distinguish recovery objectives from tolerable disruption.
Backups and alternate sites

Backups support recovery. The 3-2-1 rule of thumb means three copies, on two types of media, with one off-site. Geographic separation protects against a local disaster. Offline or appropriately immutable protection addresses a different problem: an attacker modifying or deleting backups.

An off-site copy reachable with the same compromised administrator account may still be lost. Separate administration, retention controls and tested restoration matter. Check that recovery documentation and required keys remain available during an outage. Neither a backup job's success message nor a provider's promise substitutes for an observed restore test.

Good backups can reduce pressure to pay for decryption. They do not erase data already stolen, resolve legal obligations or guarantee a clean recovery. CISA's ransomware guide covers prevention, data theft and recovery together.

For systems that can't tolerate much downtime, recovery relies on an alternate site, a second location ready to take over. These come in flavours by cost and readiness: a hot site is fully equipped and running, ready in minutes; a cold site is just space and power you'd have to build out, cheap but slow; a warm site sits in between. Which you choose is a risk-and-cost decision: the cost-benefit reasoning of the previous chapter, applied to recovery.
The clock and the crowd

A response plan needs separate owners for technical recovery, communication and legal assessment. Do not promise that “every breach has a 72-hour clock”. Under GDPR, the controller's regulator-notification deadline generally runs from awareness of a personal-data breach, with a risk-based exception; communication to affected people has a different threshold. Australia's NDB scheme uses its own coverage, serious-harm and assessment rules. Web Security and Data Protection sets out the distinction and primary sources.

Record when relevant facts became known and escalate promptly to the responsible adviser. Investigation may continue while notification duties are addressed. Customers need accurate information about what is known, what is uncertain and what they should do.

A ransom demand adds pressure. Payment does not guarantee restored data or deletion of stolen copies, and legal restrictions may apply. The authorised decision-makers need technical and legal advice for the actual circumstances. This book's exercises do not ask the reader to negotiate or decide a real ransom payment.
Testing the plan

One rule outweighs all the rest: an untested plan is only a hope. Recovery plans fail at the moment they're needed for depressingly ordinary reasons: the backups were running but never restored-tested and turned out to be corrupt; the recovery documentation was itself on the system that went down; the one person who knew the process had left. Every one of these is caught by rehearsing: restoring from backups for real, running tabletop exercises, walking the team through the crisis while it's still hypothetical. The organisations that recover smoothly are the ones that practised; the ones that discover their plan's flaws during the real disaster paid the worst possible price for the lesson.
Play it

Incident Zero has two modules that live in this chapter. Incident Response races you to uncover a hidden attack chain before time and budget run out; Disaster Recovery drops you into a live breach with a 72-hour notification clock and the ransom decision on the table. Reading about incident response is one thing; running one against a clock is another. → incidentzero.retroverse.studio
Where this connects

This chapter is what you do when a risk from risk management happens anyway, and the hot, warm, and cold-site choice is that chapter's cost-benefit reasoning applied. Investigation starts alongside containment; its evidence and attribution methods are taken up in cybercrime, botnets and forensics. And the breach-notification obligations here are grounded in the data-protection law of web security and data protection.
Questions to consider

1. What's the difference between business continuity and disaster recovery? Give an example of each.
  2. A company backs up nightly. Their RPO is "no more than one hour of data lost." What's wrong, and what would you change?
  3. Why do so many disaster-recovery plans fail at the moment they're needed? What single practice would most reduce that?
Rehearse the first decisions

Use Harbour's evidence cards for a 15-minute paper tabletop. Decide who acts at 09:15, 09:20 and 09:25; distinguish reporting from attribution. Calculate the rehearsal's recovery time and both printed recovery-point gaps. State what still needs checking before reconnecting. Success requires preservation alongside containment and separate treatment of exported data.

Case inputs and checks: Harbour dossier.
