blocks.html:
What an observer can learn from traffic depends on where they can see it and how it is protected.

Harbour's booking service depends on several network paths: customers reach the web application, staff use a VPN, and the application queries a database. Some traffic crosses infrastructure the centre does not control. An observer on a path may learn from traffic without compromising either endpoint. This chapter explains those observation limits and how to protect a connection.
What this chapter covers

By the end you should be able to:

  • Explain how scanning and sniffing work and what they reveal.
  • Describe what a packet capture shows, and why unencrypted traffic is so revealing.
  • Describe common network attacks (spoofing, man-in-the-middle) and their defences.
  • Explain why encryption in transit matters, and what segmentation and monitoring add.
A small network primer

A host is a device or system connected to a network. Its IP address helps route packets to it; a port helps identify a service on that host. A service is a listening application, such as a web server. DNS maps names to addresses. A switch connects devices locally; a router moves traffic between networks. A subnet groups addresses for routing purposes.

A trust boundary is where rules about access or trust change, such as between guest Wi-Fi and staff systems. A line on a drawing does not enforce that boundary: routing, filtering and access controls must implement it.
The network as an attack surface

Recall the phases of an attack from the first chapter: reconnaissance, then scanning, then gaining access. Networks are where the first two of those live. Before an attacker can exploit a system, they have to find it and learn what it's running. A network, by its nature, answers questions. Ask a machine "are you there?" and, unless told otherwise, it politely replies. Ask "what services are you running?" and its open ports announce them. Each reachable service adds an exposure to examine. Defaults vary, and a lack of response does not prove a device or service is absent.
Scanning: mapping the target

Scanning is how an attacker (or a defender auditing their own network) turns a vague target into a map. It usually happens in layers. First, find the live hosts: a sweep that asks every address on a network "are you there?" and notes who answers. Then, for each live host, find the open ports. A port is a numbered doorway, and each open one usually corresponds to a running service (a web server, a file share, a remote-login service). Finally, probe those services to learn which software and version is behind them, because a known version can be matched against known vulnerabilities from the software-security chapter.

The result is a blueprint: here are your machines, here are the doors that are open, here's the software behind each one. To an attacker, that's a shopping list. To a defender, the same scan is an audit. That is why the tools are dual-use, and why the defensive instinct is to close the doors you don't need. Every service you're not using is a door you can shut, shrinking the blueprint an attacker gets to work from.
Sniffing: reading the wire

Scanning finds the doors. Sniffing reads what goes through them. A network interface normally ignores traffic not addressed to it, but put it into a listening ("promiscuous") mode and it will capture everything it can hear: a packet capture of the raw conversations crossing the wire. A tool can decode supported protocols from the captured packets.

The phrase it can hear matters. On a switched network, another host's unicast traffic may never reach your capture interface. Promiscuous mode does not make the switch send it there. Wi-Fi capture also depends on the adapter, access-point settings and link protection. Explain the observation point before claiming what a capture reveals. Wireshark's Ethernet guidance sets out these limits.

One thing lands hardest the first time someone sees it: unencrypted application traffic can expose its contents to a listener at a suitable capture point. Older protocols were designed in a more trusting era and send everything unencrypted: the web's original HTTP, file transfer with FTP, remote login with Telnet, some email protocols. Capture that traffic and you don't just see that a conversation happened. You see its contents: the pages requested, the files moved, and the usernames and passwords typed in the clear. This is the sniffing that the authentication chapter warned about, made concrete: the strongest password in the world is worthless if it crosses the network in plain text for anyone listening to read. It is unsettling to witness, and it converts "you should use encryption" from advice into an obvious necessity.
Attacks in the middle

Listening is passive. Network attacks get more dangerous when the attacker stops observing and starts interfering.

Spoofing is forging an identity on the network: sending traffic that claims to come from an address that isn't yours. An attacker might spoof a trusted machine's address to slip past a filter, or forge the source of an attack to hide their tracks. The network's willingness to believe what packets claim about themselves is the weakness being exploited.

The more powerful move is the man-in-the-middle (or on-path) attack: the attacker positions themselves between two parties, so that everything each side sends passes through them first. If the protocol lacks effective authenticated protection, they may read or alter the conversation: changing a bank account number in transit, injecting malicious content, or capturing credentials as they flow past. Two common techniques get an attacker into that position on a local network. ARP spoofing tricks nearby machines into routing their traffic through the attacker by lying about which hardware address belongs to which machine. DNS spoofing answers a name lookup with the wrong address, so the victim connects to the attacker's server while believing it's the real one. The details matter less than the shape: the attacker exploits the small, trusting mechanisms that make a network convenient, and turns them into a wiretap.
Why the local attacker is special

Notice that ARP spoofing and casual sniffing both require the attacker to be on the same network. This is why an attacker who has gained a foothold on your local network, or who is sharing the coffee-shop Wi-Fi, can do things a purely remote attacker cannot. They can hear the local chatter, impersonate local machines, and slip into the middle of local conversations in ways that someone out on the wider internet, several routers away, cannot manage. It's a concrete reason the inside of a network can never be treated as automatically safe. This is the assume-breach mindset applied to your own LAN.
Defences: making the wire private again

The good news is that the central weakness, traffic readable by anyone listening, has a decisive fix, and you already met it.

Encryption in transit is the answer to sniffing. When traffic is encrypted (the web's HTTPS, which is HTTP wrapped in the TLS scheme from the cryptography chapter), an eavesdropper still captures the packets but sees only unreadable ciphertext. The credentials, the page contents, the files: all gibberish to anyone without the key. It protects the encrypted contents, but packet timing, sizes and some addressing information remain observable. Protocol and configuration choices determine what else is visible. TLS must also authenticate the intended endpoint to resist an active impostor; ignoring certificate errors undermines that check. That is why the migration of the web from HTTP to HTTPS was one of the most important security improvements of the last decade, and why sending anything sensitive over an unencrypted protocol is now indefensible.

Two more layers back it up. Segmentation divides a network into zones with controlled routes between them, so that a foothold in one part doesn't grant free movement across the whole. It's the same idea that starves a worm (from the malware chapter) and contains an incident (from the planning chapter). Monitoring watches network traffic for the tell-tale signs of trouble (a host scanning its neighbours, traffic to a known-bad address, a volume spike), so that the intrusion you couldn't prevent is at least detected, feeding straight into the incident response of the previous chapter. Encryption hides the contents, segmentation limits the movement, and monitoring catches what gets through. No single one is enough.
Play it

Incident Zero's Network Building module makes you buy an architecture you can't fully afford, and the gaps you leave come back to bite in later rounds. It's a quick, concrete lesson in why security is a budget problem as much as a technical one. → incidentzero.retroverse.studio
Where this connects

The credentials a sniffer harvests are the ones authentication taught you to protect, and encryption in transit is what stops them leaking. That encryption is the hybrid TLS scheme from cryptography, in action. And the next chapter, VPN and firewalls, covers the two defences that build on this one: a firewall to control what traffic is allowed, and a VPN to protect traffic within its configured tunnel.
Questions to consider

1. Name one everyday thing you do online that would be visible in plaintext to someone sniffing the network, and one that wouldn't. What's the difference between them?
  2. Why can an attacker on the same network do things a purely remote attacker can't?
  3. Imagine you captured your own device's traffic for one minute. What do you think you'd be able to read, and what would be hidden? What does that difference tell you about how you should send sensitive information?
State what an observer can see

In 10 minutes, draw Harbour's public, staff, guest and database boundaries. For a passive observer at the guest access point, distinguish encrypted content from routing/timing information and unknown visibility. Do not assume the observer receives every staff packet. Name a boundary test you would request from an authorised administrator; do not run it yourself.

Case inputs and checks: Harbour dossier.

A firewall decides what traffic to let through. Writing a good rule is harder than it sounds, and that difficulty is the lesson.

The last chapter left us with two problems: networks let attackers reach systems they shouldn't, and they let attackers read traffic they shouldn't. This chapter is about the two classic defences that answer those problems. A firewall controls what traffic is allowed to pass. It decides who gets to reach what. A VPN protects traffic in transit. It makes the readable wire private again. Both are everyday tools, and both are widely misunderstood. Understanding what each does and does not do is worth more than knowing how to configure either.
What this chapter covers

By the end you should be able to:

  • Explain what a firewall does and the difference between packet-filtering, stateful, and application-layer firewalls.
  • Reason about firewall rules: default-deny vs default-allow, and why order matters.
  • Explain what a VPN provides (confidentiality and integrity over an untrusted network) and what it does not.
  • Describe defence in depth in a network context: no single control trusted alone.
What a firewall does

A firewall is a checkpoint. It sits at a boundary between networks (classically between a trusted internal network and the untrusted internet) and inspects the traffic trying to cross, allowing what's permitted and blocking the rest. That's the whole idea: a gate with a guard who checks each arrival against a set of rules. A firewall does not try to block everything. Firewalls run at network boundaries, on individual hosts, and increasingly in cloud environments, but the job is always the same: decide, packet by packet or connection by connection, what's allowed through.

The difficulty, and the reason this chapter exists, is that the guard is only as good as the rules they're given. A firewall doesn't understand intent; it applies your policy literally. So the security a firewall provides is the quality of the thinking that went into its rules. It's a recurring truth in this book: the tool is easy, the judgement is hard.
The three kinds of firewall

Firewalls differ in how deeply they look at traffic, and the progression is worth knowing because each level trades speed for insight.

A packet-filtering firewall is the simplest: it examines each packet's headers in isolation (source and destination address, port, protocol) and permits or blocks based on those alone. It's fast, but it has no memory. Because it looks at each packet on its own, it can't tell whether a packet is a legitimate reply to a request you made or an unsolicited probe from an attacker; both look the same in isolation.

A stateful firewall fixes that by tracking the state of connections. It remembers that you opened a connection to a web server, so it knows to allow that server's replies back in, while still blocking unsolicited inbound traffic you never asked for. This connection awareness makes it more useful, and it's the modern default for most purposes.

An application-layer firewall (or proxy) goes deeper still: it understands the actual protocol (the structure of an HTTP request, for instance) and can make decisions based on the content, not just the addresses. A web application firewall that blocks a malicious-looking request is working at this level. Deeper inspection has processing and configuration costs. Capabilities and performance depend on implementation, and encrypted content may be unavailable unless the design explicitly provides authorised inspection.
Writing the rules

The single most important decision in a firewall policy is its default stance, and it comes in two flavours. Default-deny blocks everything and permits only what you explicitly allow: a guest list. Default-allow permits everything and blocks only what you explicitly forbid: a banned list. Default-deny limits unexpected access at a defined boundary: with a banned list you can only block the threats you thought of, and attackers make their living on the ones you didn't. A guest list fails safe: anything unforeseen is denied by default. A banned list fails open, letting the unforeseen straight through. The trade-off is friction: default-deny means every legitimate need must be anticipated and allowed, which is more work and more support tickets. Test necessary service use as well as prohibited access.

Two more subtleties bite people constantly. Order matters: in the first-match model used for our paper exercise, rules are evaluated top to bottom, so a broad "allow" placed above a specific "deny" silently defeats the deny. The packet matches the allow first and is waved through before the deny is ever considered. And specificity matters: one rule written too broadly can open a hole nobody notices, and a large rule set becomes so complex that mistakes hide in it. The cost of a bad rule is not abstract; a single misordered or over-broad line is how real networks end up exposed while everyone believes the firewall has them covered.
VPNs: a private tunnel over a public network

A firewall controls what can pass. A VPN (virtual private network) protects what's already passing. It solves the plaintext problem from the last chapter by building an encrypted tunnel between configured endpoints. Traffic selected for that tunnel is protected until it reaches the other endpoint. A full-tunnel configuration and split tunnelling cover different traffic; do not assume every application, DNS request or fallback path is included. To anyone listening in between (the attacker on the coffee-shop Wi-Fi, the operator of an untrusted network), your traffic is just ciphertext. The VPN gives you confidentiality and integrity across a network you don't trust, which is what an untrusted wire otherwise denies you.

A secure VPN protocol authenticates peers, establishes keys and protects selected traffic against disclosure and undetected alteration. The mechanisms vary by protocol and configuration; some use pre-shared credentials. The cryptography chapter explains why authentication and integrity matter alongside confidentiality.
What a VPN does not do

VPNs are also the most over-sold tool in consumer security, so it's worth being precise about their limits.

A VPN protects the link between you and the VPN server. It does not make you anonymous: your traffic still emerges from the VPN server toward its real destination, and that destination still knows what you did there. It does not secure your device: malware already on your machine is unaffected by an encrypted tunnel. And it does not protect the leg beyond the VPN server. If that onward traffic is unencrypted, it's exposed again once it leaves the tunnel. A VPN is not a substitute for HTTPS. Whether a separate VPN is useful depends on the access requirement and threat model. A VPN also doesn't remove trust; it relocates it. You've stopped trusting the local network and started trusting the VPN provider, which sees routing information and any unencrypted onward traffic. Properly protected HTTPS content remains encrypted to the website; leaving the VPN tunnel does not itself reveal that content. That can be a good trade on hostile Wi-Fi and a bad one with a shady provider, but "a VPN makes you safe" is a marketing line rather than a security fact.
Defence in depth, again

Consider what each tool leaves outside its scope. A firewall controls what traffic is allowed but can't judge the intent behind traffic it permits. Malware happily tunnels out over the same port 443 your firewall allows for ordinary web browsing. A VPN protects traffic in transit but does nothing about what happens at either end. So they join the layers from the last chapter: the firewall decides what's allowed, the VPN protects what's in motion, segmentation limits how far a foothold spreads, and monitoring catches the malicious traffic that slips through a permitted door. Check that these controls fail independently where possible, and test the paths between them. More layers do not help if they share the same unchecked administrator access.
Where this connects

A firewall and a VPN are the two defences against the scanning, sniffing, and man-in-the-middle attacks of the previous chapter, network security. A secure tunnel applies the key and authentication ideas from cryptography. And the monitoring that backs up a firewall feeds the detection stage of incident response in incident and disaster planning.
Questions to consider

1. Should a firewall default to deny or default to allow? Argue the trade-off, and say which you'd choose for a company network and why.
  2. A VPN "makes you anonymous / makes you safe." What does it actually protect, and what does it not?
  3. Give one example of a second layer catching something a firewall alone would miss.
Test both directions of the policy

In 15 minutes, trace all seven flows in Harbour's paper firewall exercise. Explain the rule that decides each one. Repair the policy and repeat the tests, including legitimate service use. Success means four expected allows and three expected denies, with no broad rule defeating a later restriction. This notation is for reasoning only, not deployment.

Case inputs and checks: Harbour dossier.

A web request should expose only the data and actions its user is authorised to access.

Harbour lets customers view bookings through a browser. A mistake in how the application handles a request could expose someone else's information. This chapter connects web weaknesses to access controls and personal-data responsibilities. A vulnerability can lead to a privacy incident; discovering a flaw alone does not establish that personal data was compromised or notification is required.
What this chapter covers

By the end you should be able to:

  • Explain the most common web vulnerabilities (injection, XSS, broken authentication, session issues) at a working level.
  • Trace how a web attack unfolds, step by step.
  • Explain core data-protection obligations (privacy principles and mandatory breach notification) with the major regimes as examples.
  • Connect web weaknesses to the data-protection consequences when they're exploited.
Why the web is the front line

A web application is, almost by definition, exposed: it exists to accept requests from strangers over the internet. Every input field, URL, and uploaded file is a place where untrusted data enters your system, and the browser on the other end is a universal client you don't control. One recurring weakness is trusting input that should never be trusted. Another is failing to check what an authenticated user is allowed to do. Data arriving from a user is treated as if it were safe, and the attacker's craft is to make that data do something it was never meant to.
Injection: when data becomes commands

The archetype is injection, and its most famous form is SQL injection. A web application builds a database query using something the user typed, a search term or a login name. If the application glues the user's input into the query text, an attacker can type input that becomes part of the command itself. Instead of a username they submit a fragment that changes what the query does: turning "find the user named X" into "find every user," or worse, "delete the table." The database, unable to tell the developer's intent from the attacker's addition, obeys.

Injection generalises beyond databases. Any time untrusted input is fed into something that interprets commands (a database, the operating system, a template engine), the same flaw can appear. And the defence generalises too: keep data and code separate. Rather than build a command by pasting text together, use mechanisms (parameterised queries, prepared statements) that hand the input to the system explicitly as data, so it can never be mistaken for instructions. Validate what comes in, and give the application only the database privileges it needs, so a successful injection does less damage.
Cross-site scripting: running attacker code in your browser

Cross-site scripting (XSS) is injection aimed at the other users of a site rather than its database. It is worth understanding because it explains how an attacker ends up running code in your browser without ever touching your machine.

A site lets users submit content (a comment, a profile, a message) and displays it back to other users. If the site fails to treat that content as untrusted, an attacker can submit a small script instead of ordinary text. When another user views the page, their browser receives that script as part of the trusted site's page and runs it in the site's context, with the victim's session. Now the attacker's code, executing as if it were the site itself, may read an accessible session token, act as them, redirect them, or deface what they see. The victim did nothing wrong except visit a page they had every reason to trust. The defence mirrors injection: treat all user content as untrusted, and encode it for the output context so the browser treats it as data. HTML text, attributes, URLs and scripts have different rules; safe framework facilities and sanitisation are needed where rich content is deliberately allowed. OWASP's XSS guidance explains why one universal escaping function is insufficient.
Authentication and session weaknesses

The web has a structural quirk that creates its own class of attacks. The protocol underneath is stateless: each request stands alone, with no memory of the last. So after you log in, the server issues a session token (usually stored in a cookie) that your browser sends with every subsequent request to say "it's still me." That token is your authenticated session. Anyone who steals it can impersonate you without ever knowing your password. This is session hijacking, and it's why the sniffing and XSS attacks in this book are so dangerous: they're often after the token rather than the password. A related trick, session fixation, has the attacker plant a session identifier they already know, then wait for the victim to log in under it. The defences are concrete: send tokens only over HTTPS so they can't be sniffed, flag cookies so scripts can't read them and they don't leak, issue a fresh token at login, and expire and revoke sessions so a stolen one does not remain useful indefinitely. An HttpOnly cookie prevents JavaScript reading that cookie; injected code may still cause authenticated actions. Cookie flags do not make an XSS flaw harmless.
A valid login is not permission

Suppose Harbour's customer page accepts a booking identifier. A customer changes that identifier and receives another person's booking. The login may be genuine and the query parameter safely handled; the missing check is whether this customer is allowed to access that record.

Enforce ownership and role checks server-side on every relevant request. Hiding a button is not access control. Test both a permitted action and an attempt by a different account that should be denied. OWASP's access-control guidance describes this distinction.
The other side: protecting the data

Behind every one of these attacks is data. Increasingly it is personal data, and the law now requires its protection. Modern data-protection law sets out principles for handling personal information that recur across jurisdictions: collect only what you need and only lawfully; use it only for the purpose you stated; keep it accurate; secure it; don't retain it longer than necessary; and let people see and correct what you hold about them. Australia codifies these as the Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) under its Privacy Act; the EU's GDPR is another version of the same pattern; other countries have their own. The names differ; the shape is consistent. The point for a defender is that security is written into the law. The applicable duties depend on the organisation, data and jurisdiction. A breach warrants investigation; its occurrence alone does not establish that every relevant legal duty was violated.

When it breaks: breach notification

A technical finding starts an assessment, not an automatic notification verdict. Identify the information, the affected people, what occurred, and which laws cover the organisation. Record uncertainty and involve the responsible privacy adviser promptly.

Australia: NDB scheme. For covered entities, an eligible breach generally involves unauthorised access or disclosure, or loss likely to lead to it, where serious harm to an individual is likely. Successful remedial action and exceptions can affect notification. Suspected eligible breaches need assessment: take all reasonable steps to complete it within 30 calendar days. Once there are reasonable grounds to believe an eligible breach occurred, notify the OAIC and relevant individuals as soon as practicable. Thirty days is not a general waiting period. OAIC's guidance

EU: GDPR. A controller notifies the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal-data breach, unless it is unlikely to pose a risk to people's rights and freedoms. A likely high risk generally requires communication to affected individuals without undue delay, subject to exceptions. Processors notify the controller without undue delay. Document breaches and decisions even where regulator notification is not required. EDPB's notification guidance

These educational summaries were checked in September 2026. They are not a complete statement of the law; other sectoral or contractual obligations may also apply. For a real incident, use the current rules and authorised legal advice.
From a web flaw to a decision

A report that one customer can read another's booking establishes an access control problem. Logs showing an unauthorised bulk export add evidence of exposure. Whether notification is required still depends on coverage, information involved, risk or harm thresholds and remedial action.

At Harbour, preserve the export evidence and escalate to the privacy adviser. Do not equate a successful restore with resolution of disclosure, or a lack of actor attribution with a lack of harm. The task is to make a supported, timely decision while technical investigation continues.
Where this connects

This chapter connects to several others. Authentication is central because the session tokens attacked here are how the web remembers you are logged in, and stealing one sidesteps the password. Network security matters because sniffing and man-in-the-middle attacks are common ways session tokens get stolen, which is why HTTPS matters. Incident & disaster planning shares the breach-notification clock here, the same one that drives a real breach response.
Questions to consider

1. In plain words, how does a cross-site scripting attack end up running an attacker's code in your browser, on a site you trust?
  2. A company is breached and customer data leaks. Under a mandatory breach-notification scheme, what are they obliged to do, and why does that obligation exist at all?
  3. If an attacker steals your active session token, what can they do that they couldn't with just your username, and what, if anything, can they still not do?
Separate three decisions

In 15 minutes, distinguish a reported access-control flaw, the supplied bulk-export evidence, and a legally notifiable breach. Record what Harbour's privacy adviser knows and must still establish. Then contrast the Australian and EU paths using the sources above. Success means no automatic 72-hour rule for every incident, and no claim that a restore resolves disclosure.

Case inputs and checks: Harbour dossier.
Take it to the AI

Optional: attempt the paper task first. Use only the fictional case, never real messages, credentials, personal information or internal logs. Check any external claims against the primary sources; do not deploy generated rules.

Act as a reviewer of an educational notification decision, not as my legal adviser. Use Harbour's fictional facts. Separate what is known, what remains uncertain, and which current regulator source addresses the uncertainty. Do not turn a vulnerability report into proof of a notifiable breach. Ask me to justify my decision before offering your assessment.

blocks.prompt: A customer portal has a login form, a search box that feeds a database query, and an admin page on the same public host. The firewall allows all outbound traffic. The team asks what to fix first. Choose the response you would defend.

options.label: Put admin behind the VPN and parameterise the queries
options.outcome: The admin surface leaves the public network, and the database stops treating input as code. Two independent controls address two different failure modes.
options.feedback: Fix the injection and reduce the exposed surface. A WAF or a secret URL alone leaves the root cause.

options.label: Move the admin page to a secret URL
options.outcome: The page is harder to guess. It is still public, still reachable, and the search box still builds SQL from input.
options.feedback: A secret URL is obscurity, not access control. The injection is untouched.

options.label: Add a WAF and leave the code alone
options.outcome: The WAF blocks some known patterns. The query remains unsafe, and any bypass or new encoding reaches the database.
options.feedback: A WAF is a useful layer, not a substitute for parameterised queries.

options.label: Disable the firewall to simplify testing
options.outcome: Testing gets easier and the estate gets more exposed. You have removed a control while investigating another.
options.feedback: Never remove a control to make a test easier. Test the policy from both sides instead.

blocks.html:
Many attacks are a business. Understanding who profits, and how, helps explain the choices defenders face.

Many financially motivated attacks involve a market of specialists selling access, malware and services. Understanding that market helps explain why a compromised ordinary device can matter. Other adversaries may seek espionage, disruption or personal harm, so financial incentives are one lens, not a complete threat model.

This chapter uses the malware vocabulary from chapter 2, then concentrates on evidence: what an observation supports, what it merely suggests, and what additional information an investigator would need.
What this chapter covers

By the end you should be able to:

  • Explain what a botnet is, and how one is built and monetised.
  • Describe the cybercrime economy: the division of labour behind modern attacks.
  • Explain, at a high level, how a real botnet works (credential-stealing and IoT examples).
  • Connect forensic traces to the attribution of an attack, and explain chain of custody.
Cybercrime is a business

The single most useful shift in thinking is to treat serious cybercrime as commerce. Attackers have costs, revenues, competitors, and customers. They reinvest profits, offer support, build reputations, and specialise. Specialisation is more efficient, just as in any legitimate economy. Cryptocurrency can help move value across borders, but public-ledger transactions may also provide an investigative trail. Traceability depends on the system and available evidence. The result is a mature underground market where almost any capability can be bought.

Seeing crime as business reframes defence. You don't have to make an attack impossible. For opportunistic profit-driven attacks, raising costs and reducing returns can discourage targeting. That does not guarantee deterrence. Raise the attacker's cost, lower their expected return, and much of the volume moves to an easier target. A great deal of security is about not being the cheapest victim on the market.
The division of labour

The defining feature of the modern cybercrime economy is that participants can specialise rather than doing the whole job. The work is split among specialists, each selling to the next. Malware developers write and sell the tools, often as polished kits with updates and customer support. Initial access brokers specialise in breaking in, then sell the foothold, access to an already-compromised company, to whoever wants to use it. Infrastructure providers rent out "bulletproof" hosting and the command servers that run attacks. Ransomware-as-a-service operators lease their ransomware to affiliates, who run the attacks and hand back a cut. Money mules and launderers turn stolen funds into clean, spendable cash.

This specialisation has three consequences, and they explain why cybercrime is so stubborn. It lowers the barrier to entry: you no longer need to be a skilled hacker to launch an attack, you can rent the capability. It makes the ecosystem resilient: arrest one malware author and the access brokers, hosts, and launderers all carry on, and a competitor fills the gap. And it muddies attribution: with so many hands touching an attack, working out who is responsible is hard. A disruption may leave other participants able to rebuild or reuse parts of the operation.
Botnets: crime at scale

Chapter 2 introduced a botnet: compromised devices under remote control through a command-and-control channel. Here the important distinction is between a device's own data and its value as infrastructure. A device can supply traffic, computing capacity or a relay even when its owner believes it has nothing worth stealing.

A single device can still be valuable, for example because of its accounts or network position. Scale adds other uses such as distributed denial of service. A defender should consider both individual compromise and the harm a fleet can cause to others.
How they work: two patterns

Two well-known cases show the pattern without needing any perishable statistics.

Gameover Zeus, a member of the Zeus family, was used for credential theft and fraud. The FBI's 2014 account of its disruption shows why a response can involve investigators, service providers and affected device owners. Disrupting infrastructure and cleaning infected devices are different parts of the work.

Mirai recruited internet-connected devices, including cameras and routers, using weak or default credentials. The US Department of Justice's account of the 2017 guilty pleas provides a historical source. For a defender, unmanaged devices and default credentials belong in the asset inventory even when their owners do not think of them as computers.
Following the trail: forensics and attribution

When an attack succeeds, the work shifts to investigation: digital forensics, the discipline of reconstructing what happened from the traces left behind. And attackers leave more traces than they'd like. System and network logs may record activity. File timestamps and document metadata can suggest a sequence, but can be modified. Some email headers are trustworthy only as far as the systems that added them; sender-supplied fields can be forged. Check clock offsets, collection context and corroborating observations. From fragments like these an investigator builds a timeline: a defensible account of who did what, and when.

Two ideas make forensics a discipline rather than a rummage. The first is chain of custody: evidence handling should make integrity and provenance open to examination: who touched it, when, and how, in an unbroken record. Poor handling can undermine confidence and admissibility. A digest shows whether a captured item changed relative to a recorded value; it does not prove the original item was truthful or identify its author. (This is the hard lesson the game module makes you feel.) The second is that attribution is difficult. The same division of labour and the same botnets that power attacks also hide the people behind them: traffic routed through a botnet appears to come from innocent victims, infrastructure is rented and disposable, and false clues are sometimes planted deliberately. Careful defenders talk about attribution in terms of confidence, not certainty.

Choose the next investigative step for its relevance and reliability, not because one kind of trace is always the clue attackers forget. Preserve the supplied material and document collection, access and interpretation. Investigation supports containment and recovery as well as later attribution; it need not wait until systems are restored. NIST's incident-response guidance provides the wider operational context.
Play it

Incident Zero's Forensics module has you chase attribution and rebuild a timeline while protecting the chain of custody. Mishandle the evidence trail and you lose the case, even when you know who did it. → incidentzero.retroverse.studio
Where this connects

This chapter connects to several others. Software security & malware supplies the weapons this economy trades in: the trojans, worms, and ransomware from that chapter. Network security matters because a botnet's command-and-control and DDoS traffic are what network monitoring exists to spot. Forensics supports the containment and recovery decisions in incident and disaster planning, as well as subsequent review.
Questions to consider

1. Why is a botnet so much more valuable to a criminal than a single compromised machine?
  2. Modern cybercrime has a "division of labour": different people write malware, sell access, rent servers, and cash out. Why does that specialisation make attacks so hard to stop?
  3. Choose one trace from Harbour's evidence cards. What does it support, what can it not establish, and what would you check next?
Annotate an evidence trail

In 15 minutes, annotate Harbour's evidence cards as observation, inference or unknown. Explain what supports concern about an export and why an account name is not an actor identity. Write a handling record with collector, time, item, digest reference and access history. Success means a defensible timeline with uncertainty visible, not a confident name to blame.

Case inputs and checks: Harbour dossier.

A useful defence makes mistakes easier to report and less costly to survive.

Security depends on people using and maintaining systems under ordinary working pressures. A login prompt, an urgent request or an unclear warning can put the wrong decision within easy reach. The design question is what happens next: can the person get help, and do other controls limit the harm?

This chapter brings together usable procedures, independent verification and a cautious assessment of AI's effects. The final chapter applies those ideas to the complete defender's dossier.
What this chapter covers

By the end you should be able to:

  • Explain how human decisions interact with system design, and why blame alone does not repair a weakness.
  • Describe social engineering and phishing, and the defences that actually work.
  • Reason about how non-technical people make security decisions with the information they're given.
  • Discuss emerging trends, including AI's double role as both a tool for attackers and a tool for defenders.
The weakest link, and why blaming the user fails

Calling people the weakest link treats a complex system as a single chain. More usefully, ask what the interface, permissions and work process made likely. The claim that "the users are the weakest link" is a trap: a framing that excuses bad security. When a well-crafted phishing email fools an employee, the instinct is to blame the employee: they should have known better. But look closer. They were doing their job, quickly, inside a system that made the wrong action easy, the right action unclear, and the difference between the two nearly invisible. Blaming the person lets the system off the hook. A team that blames users stops fixing the thing they could fix.

A more useful stance examines the system. People will make mistakes. That is a constant, and good security is designed around it rather than trying to train it away. This is assume breach applied to human beings: assume that, sooner or later, someone will be fooled, and build so the organisation survives it. That single shift, from "make users perfect" to "make mistakes survivable", is the difference between security that works and security that just apportions blame after the fact.
Social engineering and phishing

Social engineering is hacking the human instead of the machine: manipulating a person into doing what the attacker wants. It works because it targets the mental shortcuts we all rely on to get through the day. An attacker invokes authority ("this is IT, we need your password"), urgency ("the account will be closed in an hour"), fear, trust, or plain helpfulness. The victim, trying to be efficient and cooperative, complies. They are usually behaving well by the ordinary rules of work; the attacker has pointed those good instincts in the wrong direction.

Phishing is social engineering at scale: the deceptive email or message, cast wide, that lures people into revealing credentials or running malware. Spear-phishing is the targeted, personalised version aimed at a specific person, and it is more convincing. These attacks succeed because they exploit how humans are built to work. Their victims are not foolish.

The defences that help are instructive, because the obvious one is the weakest. Awareness training matters, but you cannot train people to be perfect forever, and a defence that requires every human to be vigilant every time will eventually fail. The stronger approach is to reduce the reliance on human vigilance: use technical controls that make a mistake less catastrophic. Multi-factor authentication means a phished password alone isn't enough, which is the point of the authentication chapter. Email filtering can remove some lures before they reach a person. Firm verification procedures for high-risk actions mean no single email can move money or hand over data without an independent check. Best of all is to make the safe path the easy path, so that doing the secure thing is also the convenient thing. The goal is a system in which an ordinary human error does not become a disaster, rather than a workforce that never errs.
Communicating risk to people who aren't technical

A quieter human-factors failure is that we push security decisions onto people who have no way to make them well. The classic example is the browser certificate warning. When your browser says a site's certificate can't be trusted, it is telling you something important. It could not verify you're talking to who you think you are, using the identity-proving cryptography from the cryptography chapter. That warning might be the only thing standing between you and a man-in-the-middle attacker.

Some users bypass warnings when the language is unclear, the warning interrupts urgent work, or past experience has taught them to discount it. Behaviour varies with the warning and context; do not assume most users always ignore it. This is a design failure, not the user's. A consequential security decision has been handed to someone without the information or context to make it, in words that mean nothing to them. Good security gives people clear information and, wherever possible, doesn't force impossible judgements on them.
Emerging trends: AI on both sides

AI can assist both attackers and defenders, but capability claims need a date, a task and evidence. It can lower the effort of drafting messages, summarising data or producing code. That does not make every message flawless, every exploit effective or an operation limitless.

For attackers, plausible personalised language and synthetic audio can make familiar verification shortcuts less reliable. For defenders, models may help triage reports and interpret logs, but false alarms, missed attacks and untrusted inputs still need evaluation. Logs and messages can contain hostile instructions as well as sensitive information, so an assistant must not be given authority merely because it produced a confident answer.

The NCSC assessment of AI and cyber threats to 2027 describes expected changes in attacker capability. Treat it as a dated assessment with uncertainty, not proof that every forecast has occurred.

At Harbour, an apparent manager's voice is not enough to approve an account reset or bulk export. Use a known contact route and the agreed approval process. This remains useful whether the message was written by a person or generated by a model. Give staff a reporting path that does not punish them for raising a concern that turns out to be harmless.
Where this connects

This chapter connects back across everything before it. Human decisions influence the design, operation and recovery of technical controls, so human factors belongs throughout the book. Authentication is the clearest case: MFA is a technical control that makes a human mistake survivable. And that same thread, the human running through every stage, is part of how the next chapter ties the whole book into a single lifecycle.
Questions to consider

1. "Users are the weakest link." Argue against this framing: whose fault is a successful phish, really?
  2. What does a browser certificate warning tell you? Explain why someone might bypass it and propose a safer route the organisation could offer.
  3. Give one way AI helps attackers and one way it helps defenders. Which side do you think it favours, and why?
Make reporting usable

In 10 minutes, write a response to this fictional message: “Mara here. Approve the login prompt now so I can finish the bookings.” Use a known contact route and the agreed approval process. Add a non-blaming report for someone who already approved it. Success means prompt escalation and independent verification, without using contact details supplied by the message.

Case inputs and checks: Harbour dossier.
Take it to the AI

Optional: attempt the paper task first. Use only the fictional case, never real messages, credentials, personal information or internal logs. Check any external claims against the primary sources; do not deploy generated rules.

Act as a reviewer of Harbour's reporting procedure. Use only the fictional message and case facts. Ask me what someone who already approved a prompt should do next. Then identify one obstacle in my procedure and one change that makes reporting easier without bypassing verification.

questions.prompt: Why does blaming the user fail as a security strategy?
options: It ignores the design, workload and incentives that produced the mistake
questions.explanation: A usable system and a reporting culture reduce harm more than blame does.

questions.prompt: Which combination best reduces the harm from phishing?
options: Usable reporting, MFA and a response process that acts on reports
Annual slides and a threat of discipline
questions.explanation: People will make mistakes. MFA limits the damage, and easy reporting gets help moving sooner.

questions.prompt: Why is cybercrime described as a business?
options: It has specialised roles, markets and a profit motive
It is always one person in a basement
It has no division of labour
questions.explanation: The criminal economy has builders, access brokers, operators and sellers. That division of labour explains the scale.

questions.prompt: What is a botnet?
options: A network of compromised devices controlled at scale
questions.explanation: Botnets turn many compromised machines into a coordinated capability.

questions.prompt: What matters first when investigating an incident?
options: Preserving evidence and maintaining a defensible chain of custody
Deleting the logs to save space
questions.explanation: Attribution comes later. Without preserved evidence, you cannot establish what happened.

questions.prompt: What changes when AI is available to attackers and defenders?
options: Convincing phishing and deepfakes get cheaper; verification still matters
questions.explanation: AI lowers the cost of some attacks. It does not remove the need for verification, controls or evidence.

questions.prompt: What makes a reporting culture work?
options: An easy channel, no blame for reporting and a visible response
A rule that only confirmed incidents may be reported
A single person who receives every report
A promise that nothing will be recorded
questions.explanation: People report when it is easy, safe and visibly useful. Waiting for certainty loses time.

blocks.html:
A defence plan should make its limits as visible as its controls.

You now have the pieces of a defender's dossier. The final test changes the budget and recovery target. It asks whether you can recognise an unresolved risk and explain it to the person authorised to decide. A polished plan that hides a failed test is less useful than a short one that exposes it.
What this chapter covers

By the end you should be able to:

  • Connect assets, controls, evidence and recovery decisions in one plan.
  • Check whether a changed requirement invalidates an earlier answer.
  • Distinguish a justified decision from a claim that everything is secure.
  • Assign responsibility for unresolved risk and future review.
Joining the dots

Return to the seven activities introduced in chapter 1: design, harden, detect, respond, recover, investigate, and audit/learn. Human decisions run through every activity. These are overlapping tasks, not seven departments that hand an incident along in a fixed sequence.

At Harbour, permissions influence whether a login can become a bulk export. Logging affects what the response lead can establish. Recovery credentials affect whether backups survive. A notification assessment may still be open after the service is restored. Those connections are what the dossier should make visible.

A checklist can help an authorised responder avoid missing a necessary step. It needs an owner, a context and testing. The failure is treating checked boxes as proof that the service can meet its obligations under changed conditions.
Complete the independent case

Use Harbour's weekend programme. Allow 30–45 minutes, working alone without AI. The appendix supplies every changed fact and an eight-point check. Write your answer before reading the comparison.

Your one-page decision needs the assets and permissions, an affordable control choice, risk arithmetic, allowed and denied tests, both recovery checks, an evidence-preserving response and a privacy escalation. End with what is ready, what is not, who can decide, and what evidence is needed next.

You are not required to make the constraints fit. If the stated recovery time misses the target or the budget leaves a known boundary weakness, say so. Do not create an imaginary free control to make the answer look complete. An explicit request for a changed budget, a tested improvement or a deferred launch is a legitimate result.
Check and transfer

Compare your answer with the reasoning check. Aim for seven of eight criteria, with no unsafe testing, unsupported readiness claim or missed recovery-target failure. If you disagree with the worked choice, identify the constraint and evidence that make your alternative defensible.

For a second attempt, ask another reader to change one supplied constraint. Predict which section of your dossier must change before recalculating it. That is a stronger test of understanding than repeating the original answer.
Play the whole thing

Every stage in that loop is easier to understand than to do. Doing it, under time and budget pressure, is where the judgement lives. Incident Zero, the free print-and-play game referenced throughout these chapters, has a full campaign that runs this entire lifecycle end to end: design a network, harden it, detect and respond to a breach, recover from the disaster, and investigate what happened. Playing it is the closest thing to living a security cycle in an afternoon. If this book gave you the map, the campaign lets you walk the ground. → incidentzero.retroverse.studio

The game is optional group enrichment. Its current landing page describes the player, printing and time requirements. The paper dossier above is a complete solo route and does not reproduce the game's materials.
Questions to consider

1. Which supplied fact most changed your control choice, and why?
  2. Which conclusion depends on evidence you do not yet have?
  3. What should trigger a new review after an initially acceptable plan?
Carry the decision forward

Keep the dossier as a record of a decision under stated conditions. When the system, staff, evidence or obligations change, revisit it. The useful habit is to explain what a control does, demonstrate it where possible, and make the remaining uncertainty visible to the right decision-maker.

blocks.prompt: The board asks: "Are we secure?" You have a completed dossier with two known gaps: a boundary weakness the budget did not cover, and a recovery test that missed the target. The launch date is close. Choose your response.

options.label: Present the residual risk, the evidence and the decision options
options.outcome: The board sees what is ready, what is not, who owns the remaining risk and what a changed budget or a deferred launch would buy. The decision is explicit.

effects.Launch: A board decision, not a surprise

options.feedback: A defensible answer names the limit and the owner. It does not claim the gaps away.

options.label: Say the controls are in place and the service is secure
options.outcome: The room relaxes. The boundary weakness and the failed recovery test are still there, now without an owner.
options.feedback: A claim is not evidence. The failed test is the evidence.

options.label: Adjust the recovery test so it passes
options.outcome: The dashboard turns green. The service still misses the recovery target, and the test no longer measures what the board asked about.
options.feedback: Changing the test does not change the recovery time.

options.label: Buy another security tool and call the gap closed
options.outcome: A new product is added. The boundary weakness may remain, and the recovery target is still unproven.
options.feedback: A tool is not a control until it is configured, tested and owned.

blocks.debrief: A good handover makes the limits as visible as the controls. Name the risk, the evidence, the owner and the decision you are asking the board to make.
